papers.title: Single-atom-doped zeolite electrolyte for quasi-solid-state zinc-iodine batteries
papers.abstract: Quasi-solid electrolytes can mitigate polyiodide shuttling and suppress parasitic reactions at zinc negative electrode in zinc-iodine batteries by reducing free water, but their limited liquid content often results in sluggish interfacial charge transfer. Here we show liquid-electrolyte-wetted quasi-solid electrolytes by combining single-atom-modified zeolites (single-atom = iron, cobalt, nickel, and copper) with zinc sulfate aqueous solution for high-rate zinc-iodine batteries. Theoretical calculations, in situ spectroscopy, and laser confocal microscopy reveal that the single-atom metal sites enhance iodine conversion kinetics and suppress polyiodide shuttling through a synergistic catalytic-adsorption effect, with iron-doped zeolite exhibiting the strongest performance. Iron-doped zeolite further stabilizes water molecules, suppresses side reactions, and promotes uniform zinc deposition. The iron-doped zeolite-assembled zinc-iodine batteries maintain a discharge capacity of 81.2 mAh g−1 (based on iodine mass) after 6,800 cycles at 4 A g−1, while proof-of-concept pouch cells exhibit a capacity of 147.6 mAh g−1 (based on iodine mass) or 52 mAh g−1 (based on total positive electrode mass) after 200 cycles at 0.5 A g−1. Lastly, iron-doped zeolite also demonstrates compatibility with other positive electrode materials for rechargeable zinc batteries. Quasi-solid zinc iodine batteries face sluggish kinetics due to low liquid content. Here, authors report single-atom metal-doped zeolite electrolytes that simultaneously catalyze iodine conversion, suppress polyiodide shuttling, and stabilize zinc deposition, achieving 6,800 stable cycles at high rates and demonstrating proof-of-concept pouch-cell performance.

papers.title: Chemistry-infused bandit framework for interpretable autonomous campaign of electrocatalysis
papers.abstract: Abstract Autonomous experimentation offers a time-efficient route towards accelerated catalyst discovery, but current practices often rely on black-box models that are difficult to interpret. Here we demonstrate the paradigm of interpretable autonomous exploration of a 12-dimensional space in the electrocatalytic hydrogen evolution reaction by integrating an interpretable decision-making artificial intelligence with a fully automated electrochemical platform. Guided by a human’s chemistry-informed hypothesis, a chemistry-infused bandit is established to reflect the locally quadratic approximation between synthetic conditions and electrocatalytic activities near the explored optimum region. Not only does such a decision-making bandit lead to the discovery of previously unreported, earth-abundant electrocatalysts at least comparable to Pt-based ones, the bandit also reveals model-derived hypothesis for how synthetic conditions affect the electrocatalysts’ performance near the identified local optima as autonomous inquiry proceeds, which is otherwise untenable from black-box ones. Incorporating chemistry-informed hypothesis into the decision-making bandit is generally applicable to any chemistry problem and offers a framework for autonomous investigation, advancing hypothesis generation for catalyst’s design principles beyond simple optimization.

papers.title: Nuclear magnetic resonance on a single atom with a local probe
papers.abstract: Atomic nuclear spins are promising candidates in the development of quantum information technologies on a wide variety of physical platforms. Thanks to the high degree of isolation from their environment, nuclear spins show long-lived spin states, but this also poses challenges on their control and readability. Detailed characterization and control over the atomic-scale environment of the nuclear spin become of great importance for their efficient control. In this work, using scanning tunnelling microscopy, we reveal nuclear magnetic resonance on a single on-surface atom. We employ an electron-nuclear double resonance measurement scheme and resolve nuclear spin transitions of a single 47Ti isotope with a nuclear spin of I = 5/2. Our measurements and numerical analysis reveal the nature of hyperfine and quadrupole couplings of the studied system. We also show our ability to address the nuclear spin in the limit of weak hybridization with the electron spin, a requirement for direct control of the nuclear spin in the long-lifetime regime. This investigation of an atomic nuclear spin in a platform with atomic-scale control is a valuable development for other platforms deploying nuclear spins. Nuclear magnetic resonance of individual on-surface atoms has relied on electron-nuclear spin hybridization. Here, the authors use electron-nuclear double resonance with a scanning tunnelling microscope to resolve nuclear-spin transitions of a single atom on a surface in the weak-hybridization regime.

papers.title: Particulate Metal Oxysulfides for Photocatalytic and Photoelectrocatalytic Water Splitting
papers.abstract: Narrow bandgap metal oxysulfide photo(electro)catalysts have been extensively investigated as effective candidates for solar energy conversion via water splitting using long-wavelength visible light. Up to now, considerable progress has been achieved over metal oxysulfide photo(electro)catalysts for water splitting. However, compared to metal oxide and metal sulfide photo(electro)catalysts, its performance is still inferior mainly owing to poor control in charge separation and surface catalytic conversion. To address this issue, this review is devoted to presenting a comprehensive illustration of research progress in this field. First, an overview of the fundamentals of photo(electro)catalytic water splitting systems and metal oxysulfides is provided. On this basis, the water splitting performance of representative metal oxysulfides is summarized, together with effective strategies covering material synthesis, surface modification, and system construction. Emphases are especially placed on the aspects of charge separation and surface catalytic reaction, offering promising design perspectives for advancing photo(electro)catalysts and integrated systems based on metal oxysulfides. Future prospects and challenges in developing efficient metal oxysulfide photo(electro)catalysts and their integrated systems are also discussed.

papers.title: A Cytoplasmic pH Sensor Redefines Gating in Bacterial Urea Channels and Acid Resistance
papers.abstract: Bacterial survival in acidic environments depends on urea channels like UreI, which neutralize protons after importing urea and hydrolyzing it to ammonia and carbon dioxide. While pH-dependent gating was attributed to periplasmic histidines, the role of cytoplasmic residues remained unexplored. Using yeast complementation assays, in vitro permeability measurements, systematic sequence analysis, and molecular dynamics simulations, we identify a conserved cytoplasmic glutamic acid residue (E136 in Streptococcus salivarius, E135 in Helicobacter hepaticus, E159 in Helicobacter pylori) as a pH sensor in UreI channels. Protonation of this residue disrupts its interaction with a conserved partner (R20 in S. salivarius and H. hepaticus, T170 in H. pylori), increasing cytoplasmic-loop flexibility and enhancing conformational sampling of a conserved aromatic triad in the selectivity filter, thereby facilitating urea permeation. Mutagenesis across S. salivarius, H. pylori, and H. hepaticus confirms the residue´s indispensable and conserved role, revealing a Gram-type-specific gating mechanism: Gram-positive bacteria rely solely on this glutamic acid sensor, while Gram-negative pathogens employ a dual-sensor model integrating both cytoplasmic glutamic acid and periplasmic histidines. By overturning the paradigm of exclusive periplasmic pH sensing, this work reveals a conserved yet adaptable mechanism for bacterial acid resistance, offering a new molecular target for precision antimicrobial development.

papers.title: RuO2‐Based Electrocatalysts for Acidic Oxygen Evolution: Mechanistic Origins of the Activity–Stability Trade‐Off and Pathways to Rational Design
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Ruthenium dioxide (RuO 2 ) is widely considered as a leading non‐iridium candidate for the acidic oxygen evolution reaction (OER) in proton exchange membrane water electrolysis (PEMWE), owing to its high intrinsic activity and comparatively low cost. Its practical implementation, however, is fundamentally limited by a persistent activity–stability trade‐off arising from the close coupling between oxygen evolution, lattice oxidation, and Ru dissolution under strongly acidic and oxidizing conditions. This review summarizes recent progress in RuO 2 ‐based acidic OER catalysts from a mechanism‐centered perspective, with emphasis on how electronic structure, defect chemistry, lattice oxygen reactivity, and spin‐related effects collectively govern catalytic activity, reaction pathways, and degradation behavior. We further discuss how operando characterization has advanced understanding of dynamic active states and stability limits and highlight the emerging role of high‐throughput computation, machine learning, and active learning in accelerating catalyst discovery. By integrating mechanistic understanding, materials engineering, and data‐driven design, this review aims to outline a coherent framework for the development of highly active, durable, and scalable RuO 2 ‐based catalysts for acidic water oxidation.

papers.title: Operando Identification of h‐CoSe@Co Self‐Reconstruction into a CoOOH Heterointerface as the Active Site for Alkaline Hydrogen Evolution
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Understanding the dynamic surface evolution of electrocatalysts under working conditions is essential for the rational design of efficient water‐splitting systems. Herein, the self‐induced surface reconstruction of a superstructural electrocatalyst composed of metallic cobalt/hexagonal cobalt selenide nanoparticles confined within an N‐doped carbon nanocage ( h ‐CoSe@Co) during the alkaline hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) is investigated. Upon surface reconstruction, h ‐CoSe@Co evolves into an h ‐CoSe/CoOOH heterointerface that serves as the catalytically active site, promoting water adsorption and facilitating water dissociation. In situ Raman spectroscopy enables direct observation of the surface reconstruction and interfacial water capture. Complementary density functional theory (DFT) calculations further demonstrate that the h ‐CoSe/CoOOH heterostructure exhibits redistributed electronic states near the Fermi level and a near‐thermoneutral Gibbs free energy of hydrogen adsorption. Due to the synergistic effects of surface reconstruction and intrinsic properties, h ‐CoSe@Co delivers enhanced HER performance relative to o ‐CoSe 2 and c‐ CoSe 2 . This proof‐of‐concept study provides deep insight into the structure–activity relationship of a cobalt‐based chalcogenide electrocatalyst through a self‐induced surface reconstruction strategy for tuning adsorption energetics, thereby advancing efficient hydrogen energy technologies.

papers.title: Bifunctional Platinum Cocatalysts With Directional Loading on a Covalent Organic Framework for Photocatalytic Overall Water Splitting
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Photocatalytic overall water splitting (OWS) over semiconductors is a promising strategy for converting solar energy into clean hydrogen, and rational cocatalyst design is critical for accelerating reaction kinetics. Herein, Pt nanoparticles with an average size of ∼1.5 nm were prepared by a microwave‐assisted method. By premixing Pt suspensions with 2,4,6‐trihydroxybenzene‐1,3,5‐tricarbaldehyde (Tp) and 2,2′‐bipyridine‐5,5′‐diamine (BPy) monomers before solvothermal treatment, Pt was directionally loaded onto both Tp and BPy sites of TpBPy‐COF, affording the dual‐Pt‐loaded photocatalyst Pt@TpBPy@Pt. This material efficiently drives OWS, achieving H 2 and O 2 evolution rates of 60 and 28.8 µmol g −1 h −1 , respectively. The roles of Pt at Tp and BPy were examined by selectively replacing Pt with Ag and using CrO 4 2− reduction to CrOOH as a probe reaction. CrOOH deposition on the metal anchored at the Tp end reveals that Pt at BPy sites functions as the oxidation cocatalyst, whereas Pt at Tp sites serves as the reduction cocatalyst. UPS and KPFM show that electrons extracted from H 2 O by Pt at BPy migrate through BPy to Tp and accumulate on Pt at Tp to initiate HER. This work clarifies Pt's bifunctional role and provides a strategy for designing COF‐based OWS photocatalysts.

papers.title: Interface‐Growth‐Assisted Molten Salt Synthesis of Cobalt‐Embedded Ruthenium Oxide for Oxygen Evolution Electrocatalysis
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Ruthenium oxide (RuO 2 ) is the most promising alternative to iridium oxide (IrO 2 ) catalyst in proton‐exchange‐membrane water electrolysis (PEMWE). However, its practical application has been hindered by poor stability. Here, we developed an interface‐growth‐assisted molten salt synthesis (MSS) strategy for the preparation of stable cobalt (Co)‐embedded RuO 2 (Co‐RuO 2 ) nanorods using a lanthanum cobaltate (LaCoO 3 ) template. The MSS environment is beneficial for anisotropic growth and the exposure of highly active RuO 2 crystal planes. Moreover, the in situ topological transformation arising from the interface growth of RuO 2 on LaCoO 3 can further enhance these effects and incorporate Co into the RuO 2 lattice. The PEMWE electrolyzer with Co‐RuO 2 as the anode catalyst can operate steadily for over 300 h at 500 mA cm −2 . Theoretical simulations indicate that Co substitutions would stabilize oxygen vacancies and increase metal‐oxygen covalency, thereby lowering cell voltage and improving the stability of the PEMWE electrolyzer. This work pioneers template‐directed interface growth in an MSS environment to prepare anisotropic RuO 2 catalysts for practical PEMWE applications.

papers.title: MOFs‐on‐MOFs Derived Ternary Sulfide Heterojunctions: Dynamic Ni Site Switching via Interfacial Charge Redistribution for Efficient OER and UOR Catalysis
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Bifunctional electrocatalysts simultaneously applicable for oxygen evolution reaction (OER) and urea oxidation reaction (UOR) remain limited by intrinsic active‐site incompatibility and competitive intermediate adsorption. High‐valence metal centers are required for lattice oxygen activation during OER, whereas low‐valence metallic sites are favorable for urea coordination and C─N bond cleavage in UOR, making dual‐reaction optimization difficult. Herein, a hierarchical Ni 3 S 2 /Co 3 S 4 /FeNi 2 S 4 /NF ternary sulfide heterojunction is rationally fabricated via a MOFs‐on‐MOFs strategy followed by in situ sulfidation. The tightly coupled triphase nanointerface and porous wrinkled nanoflower architecture induce intense interfacial charge redistribution, which precisely tunes the reversible oxidation‐state evolution of Ni active sites. The optimized electronic configuration endows the catalyst with outstanding bifunctional electrocatalytic performance, requiring an overpotential of 219 mV for OER and 1.30 V vs. RHE for UOR at 10 mA cm −2 . In situ spectroscopic characterizations and DFT calculations confirm reveal opposite reversible valence evolution of Ni centers: OER follows the lattice oxygen mechanism on O‐Ni 3+ ‐O sites, while urea preferentially activates on Ni 2+ sites. This interface‐driven dynamic switching of Ni active sites fundamentally resolves active‐site competition and optimizes intermediate adsorption. This work clarifies an atomic‐level dynamic adaptation mechanism of Ni‐based catalysts, offering a reliable interfacial modulation strategy for advanced bifunctional electrocatalysts.

papers.title: Karst Cave EffectInduced Dandelion‐Like Porous Cobalt–Nickel Silicate Hydroxide: Enhanced Oxygen Evolution Reaction Performance via LOM Mechanism
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Enhancing the kinetics and mass transfer efficiency is the central issue in the research of the catalytic oxygen evolution reaction (OER). Here, an in situ hydrothermal transformation method for synthesizing ultra‐porous cobalt‐nickel silicate hydroxide (CNSH) with a layered double hydroxide (LDH) is demonstrated. This in situ variation from well‐crystallized carbonate to amorphous silicate hydroxide leads to a dandelion‐like structure originating from framework reconstruction as topotactic transformation process, defined as “karst cave effect”. Moreover, the specific coordination environment in CNSH not only enhances Metal‐Oxygen Covalency (MOC) for promoting lattice oxygen‐mediated mechanism (LOM), but also improves structural stability. CNSH demonstrates superior OER performance, including low overpotentials of 275 mV and 313 mV for current densities of 10 and 100 mA cm −2 , respectively, as well as exceptional long‐term stability for 800 h at 1 A cm −2 . This work provides an innovative and feasible pathway for the rational design of electrocatalysts with both porous structure and rapid kinetics for efficient and stable water oxidation.
